Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 57, verse 16–17:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe﴾. Scholars differed regarding who this was revealed about, on two views.

The first: it was revealed concerning the believers. Ibn Mas'ud said: "Between our acceptance of Islam and being rebuked by this verse there were only four years, so the believers began rebuking one another."

The second: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. This was reported by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil said: "The hypocrites asked Salman al-Farisi, saying: 'Tell us about the Torah, for in it are wonders,' so this verse was revealed." Al-Zajjaj said: "This verse was revealed concerning a group of believers who were urged toward tenderness of heart and humility. As for those whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, described with humility and tenderness, they are a class of believers above these." According to the first view, faith (iman) is taken in its literal sense. According to the second, the meaning is: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe﴾ with their tongues. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is: has it not drawn near; one says "anā al-shay'" (the thing has come near) when it draws close.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That their hearts should humble themselves﴾, i.e., become soft and tender at the remembrance of Allah. The meaning is that remembrance should necessarily produce humility in them. ﴿And what has come down of the truth﴾. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-ma nazzala" with a fatha on the nun and zay, with the zay doubled. Nafi', Hafs, and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "nazala" with a fatha on the nun and a light zay. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-'Aliyah, Ibn Ya'mar, Yunus ibn Habib from Abu 'Amr, and Aban from 'Asim read "nuzzila" with a damma on the nun, a kasra on the zay, and the zay doubled. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Raja' read "wa-ma anzala" with an open hamzah and a fatha on the zay. Abu Mijlaz and 'Amr ibn Dinar read it likewise, except with a damma on the hamzah and a kasra on the zay. "Al-haqq" means the Qur'an. ﴿And that they should not be﴾: Ruways from Ya'qub read "la takununu" with a ta' (i.e., "lā takūnū" in the second person). ﴿Like those who were given the Book﴾, meaning the Jews and the Christians. ﴿So the term grew long for them﴾, and the term (al-amad) is the period of time. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-amad means the end point. The meaning is that their time with the prophets and the righteous became distant. ﴿So their hearts hardened, and many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾, and these are those who did not believe in 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. ﴿Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death﴾, i.e., He brings forth plants from it after its dryness, and likewise He is able to revive the dead. ﴿We have certainly made clear to you the signs﴾, which indicate His oneness and power. ﴿That you might reason﴾, i.e., so that you may reflect.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 57, verses 18–19:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity﴾ — Ibn Kathir and ʿĀṣim (except Ḥafs) read it with the ṣād lightened in both places (al-muṣaddiqīna, al-muṣaddiqāt), according to the meaning of "affirming belief" (al-taṣdīq). The rest read it with the ṣād doubled (al-muṣṣaddiqīna, al-muṣṣaddiqāt), according to the meaning of "giving charity" (al-ṣadaqa).

(p-170) His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the truthful (al-ṣiddīqūn) and the martyrs (al-shuhadāʾ) with their Lord﴾ — the scholars differed concerning the structure of the verse, on two views.

The first: the sentence is complete at His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the truthful (al-ṣiddīqūn)﴾, and then He begins, saying: ﴿And the martyrs are with their Lord﴾. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Masruq, al-Farraʾ, and others.

The second: the verse is kept in its own arrangement, and the waw in "wal-shuhadāʾ" is the waw of conjunction (waw al-nasaq). Then, concerning its meaning, there are two views.

The first: every believer is a ṣiddīq and a shahīd. This was said by Ibn Masʿud and Mujahid.

The second: it was revealed concerning a specific group, namely eight men who were the first to embrace Islam: Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, ʿAli, Hamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, Talha, al-Zubayr, Saʿd, and Zayd. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥak. Concerning the shuhadāʾ there are two views.

The first: that it is the plural of shāhid (witness). Then among them there are two views. The first: that they are the prophets specifically (p-171), said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: that they are the witnesses before their Lord against themselves by faith in God, said by Mujahid.

The second view: that it is the plural of shahīd (martyr), said by al-Ḍaḥḥak and Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 57, verses 20–21:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Know that the life of this world is but play and amusement﴾. He means: the life in this abode is "play and amusement," i.e., deception that passes away quickly. Some of the exegetes (mufassirun) held that what is indicated by this is the state of the disbeliever in his worldly life, because his life passes in amusement, play and the adornment of the world. He boasts before his companions and neighbours, and vies with them in wealth and children. He gathers wealth from other than its lawful source, and he exalts himself over the friends of Allah by his wealth, his servants and his son. So his lifetime is spent on these things, and he does not turn to working for the Hereafter. Then He made a comparison for this life, saying: ﴿like the likeness of rain﴾, i.e., rain, ﴿whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers﴾, and they are the farmers. They were called disbelievers (kuffar) because when the sower casts the seed into the earth, he "covers" it (kafara), i.e., conceals it, and its "vegetation" (nabatuhu), i.e., what grows from that rain, ﴿then it dries up﴾, i.e., it becomes dry (yayba), ﴿and you see it turning yellow﴾ after its greenness and freshness, ﴿then it becomes debris﴾, i.e., it crumbles and breaks after its dryness. The explanation of this parable has already been given in Surah Yunus at His saying, the Exalted: (p-172) ﴿Indeed, the likeness of the life of this world is like the water which We send down from the sky﴾ [verse 24], and in Surah al-Kahf at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And present to them the example of the life of this world﴾ [verse 45].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And in the Hereafter is severe punishment﴾, i.e., for the enemies of Allah, ﴿and forgiveness from Allah and approval﴾ for His friends and the people of His obedience. What follows this is mentioned in [Al 'Imran: 185] up to His saying: ﴿That is the bounty of Allah﴾, whereby He explains that no one enters Paradise except by the bounty of Allah.

**Poetry:**

؎ No, by Him whose servant I am in His worship, and man in this age is a target of calamity and sorrow.

؎ What would please me is that my camels are in their pastures, and what has come to pass by the decree of the Lord of creation, let it be.

What follows this has been mentioned in Surat an-Nisa' [4:37], and what was said there about stinginess is what is said here, up to His words: ﴿And whoever turns away﴾, i.e., from faith, ﴿then indeed Allah is the Free of need﴾ from His servants, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾ to His friends. The meaning of the two names has already passed under [al-Baqarah 2:267] (p-174). Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿Indeed Allah, the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ without "huwa" (He), and likewise it is in the codices (masahif) of the people of Madina and Syria.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 57, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs﴾, i.e., with signs and arguments. ﴿And We sent down with them the Book﴾ with the explanation of the sacred laws (shara'i') and the rulings (ahkam). Regarding "the Balance" (al-Mizan) there are two opinions.

The first: that it is justice (al-'adl). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The second: that it is that by which things are weighed. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Muqatil. According to the first opinion, the meaning is: and We commanded justice. According to the second: and We placed the Balance, i.e., We commanded it. ﴿That mankind may maintain justice﴾, i.e., so that they may uphold justice.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We sent down iron﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: that God, may He be exalted, sent down with Adam the anvil (sindan), the tongs (kalbatan), and the hammer (mitraqah). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that the meaning of "sent down" (anzalna) is "brought into being and created," as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He sent down for you of the cattle eight pairs﴾ [az-Zumar: 6].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In it is severe might﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: this is because one defends oneself with it and fights with it. ﴿And benefits for mankind﴾ in their tools and what they benefit from, such as vessels and other things.

(p-175) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that Allah may know﴾. This is connected to His saying: ﴿that mankind may maintain justice﴾. The meaning: that people may deal with justice, and that Allah may know ﴿who supports Him﴾ by fighting in His way and supporting His religion. This is because He commanded that in the Book which He sent down. The meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that Allah may know﴾ has already been explained in several places. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in the unseen﴾, i.e., while they have not seen Allah, nor the rulings of the Hereafter; rather, one strives and is rewarded for obeying in the unseen.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 57, verse 26–27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We placed in their descendants prophethood and the Scripture﴾ — meaning: the books. "Among them" — meaning: among the descendants — ﴿are those who are guided, but many of them are defiant transgressors﴾. Concerning this there are two statements.

The first: "disbelievers" (kafirun); this is related from Ibn Abbas. The second: "disobedient" (ʿasun); this is related from Muqatil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We sent, following in their footsteps﴾ — that is, We caused to follow in the footsteps of Nuh, Ibrahim, and their descendants — "with Isa," and he was the last of the prophets of the Children of Israel. ﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him﴾ — meaning: the disciples (al-Hawariyyun, "the disciples") and others of his followers upon his religion — "compassion" (ra'fah), whose meaning has already been explained [An-Nur: 2] — "mutual affection," just as Allah, exalted is He, described the companions of our Prophet, peace be upon him, when He said: ﴿compassionate among themselves﴾ [Al-Fath: 29].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But monasticism, they invented it﴾ — this is not coordinated with what precedes it; rather it is in the accusative by an implied verb, indicated by what follows it, its estimate being: "and they invented monasticism which they invented" — that is, they brought it from their own selves. It is their excessiveness in worship, imposing hardships upon themselves by abstaining from food, drink, clothing and marriage, and devoting themselves to worship in the mountains. ﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾ — that is, We did not impose it upon them. Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ there are two statements.

The first: that it refers back to His saying ﴿they invented it﴾, and its estimate is: "We did not prescribe it for them, except that they invented it seeking the pleasure of Allah." This was mentioned by Ali ibn Isa and al-Rummani, from Qatadah and Zayd ibn Aslam.

The second: that it refers back to His saying ﴿We did not prescribe it﴾. Then, concerning the meaning of the statement, there are two views. The first: "We did not prescribe it for them after they entered into it voluntarily, except seeking the pleasure of Allah." Al-Hasan said: "They volunteered to invent it, then Allah prescribed it for them." Al-Zajjaj said: "When they obligated themselves to that voluntary act, it became necessary for them to complete it, just as when a person makes a fast binding upon himself, it is not made obligatory on him, but he must complete it." Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: "Innovation (al-ibtida') may be by speech, such as when one vows or makes something obligatory upon oneself, and it may be by action, by entering into it. The general wording of the verse includes both matters, so this requires that whoever innovates an act of worship, whether by speech or by action, is obligated to observe it and complete it." The second: the meaning is: "We did not command them with it except with what pleases Allah, azza wa jall, and nothing else." This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾ — concerning those referred to there are two statements.

The first: that they are those who invented monasticism; this is the view of the majority. Then, concerning the meaning of the statement, there are three views. The first: that they did not observe it in order to alter and change their religion; this was said by Atiyyah al-Awfi. The second: due to their negligence in what they had obligated upon themselves. The third: due to their disbelief in the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, when he was sent; al-Zajjaj mentioned both statements.

The second: that they are those who followed the innovators of monasticism in their monasticism, not observing it by following the path of its originators. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related this meaning from Ibn Abbas.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We gave those among them who believed their reward﴾ — concerning them there are three statements.

The first: those who believed in Muhammad; ﴿and many of them are defiant transgressors﴾ — and they are those who did not believe in him.

The second: that those who believed are the believers in Isa, and the defiant transgressors are the polytheists.

The third: that those who believed are the innovators of monasticism, and the defiant transgressors are those who followed them in a manner not conforming to the correct rule.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 57, verses 28–29:

(p-178) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger﴾. The majority of the exegetes hold that this address is to the Jews and the Christians. The meaning is: O you who have believed in Moses and Jesus, fear Allah, and believe in His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿He will give you two portions﴾, i.e., two shares and two lots, ﴿of His mercy﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: al-kifl (portion) is a cloth that keeps the rider from falling. So the meaning is: He will give you two shares that will protect you from the destruction of sins. We have already explained the meaning of "al-kifl" in Surat al-Nisa' [4:85]. Regarding what is meant by "two portions" here, there are two opinions.

One: for their belief in the prophets who came before, and the other for their belief in Muhammad (ﷺ). This is said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: one of them is the reward of this world, and the other is the reward of the Hereafter. This is said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And will make for you a light﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions. (p-179) One: the Qur'an, related by Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: a light by which you walk upon the Path, related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. The third: guidance, said by Mujahid. The fourth: faith, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So that the People of the Scripture may know﴾. The "la" (not) is extra. This is said by al-Farra': the Arabs make "la" a connective in every speech in which a negation has entered at its end or its beginning. This is one of those in which a negation has been placed at its end. The meaning is: so that the People of the Scripture who did not believe in Muhammad may know ﴿that they have no power over anything of Allah's bounty﴾, i.e., that they have no power over anything of Allah's bounty. The meaning is that He made the two rewards for whoever believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), so that whoever did not believe in him may know that they have no reward and no share in Allah's bounty, ﴿and that bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills﴾, so He gave it to the believers. This is a summary of the opinion of the majority regarding these two verses. However, a group has held that when the verse was revealed concerning the Muslims among the People of the Book, ﴿those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾, up to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾ [28:52–54], they boasted over the Muslims about the increase in reward, and this grieved the Muslims, so these two verses were revealed. This meaning is in the narration of Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Muqatil also said it. According to this, the address is to the Muslims, and the meaning is: He will give you two rewards so that the believers among the People of the Book may know that they have no power over anything of Allah's bounty that He has granted you specifically, for He has favored you over all creation. Qatadah said: when the words of Allah, Exalted is He, ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger...﴾ were revealed, the People of the Book envied the Muslims for it, so Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿So that the People of the Book may know﴾, the verse.

According to this, the address is to the Muslims, and the meaning is: He will give you two rewards so that the believers among the People of the Book may know that they have no power over anything of Allah's bounty that He has granted you specifically, for He has favored you over all creation. Qatadah said: when the words of Allah, Exalted is He, ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger...﴾ were revealed, the People of the Book envied the Muslims for it, so Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿So that the People of the Book may know﴾, the verse.
